notes.claim: The synchronous speed of the turning field is 120 f / p rpm for f hertz and p poles; an induction motor's shaft runs a little slower than it.
In a series motor the same current flows through field and armature, and its speed can climb to dangerous levels if it runs without a load.
A motor that is turning also acts as a generator; the emf it makes is called back emf and it opposes the supply.
Three windings 120 electrical degrees apart, each fed from one phase, make one combined magnetic field that turns at a constant speed, the synchronous speed.
The turning field cuts the short-circuited rotor conductors and induces a current in them; that current makes its own field, which interacts with the stator field to give torque.

The rotor has to turn slower than the field: with no speed difference there is no cutting, so no current is induced and no torque is produced. An induction motor can approach synchronous speed but never reach it.
Slip is the difference between synchronous and actual speed, normally written as a percentage. Load makes the rotor slow and slip grow; taking load off lets it speed up and slip shrink.
Synchronous speed is 120 f / p rpm for f hertz and p poles.
Full-load slip of a cage motor is a few percent: about 2 to 3% (one maker) and under 5% (another).
Starting from the supply direct, a motor draws usually 6 to 8 times its rated current and can draw more than 10 times.
For a small motor (up to about 30 kW) ABB's 2010 handbook gives a direct-on-line starting torque of 1.5 to 2.5 times rated; its 2004 edition gave 2.5 to 3. The figure is a range.
Swapping the supply connections on any two of the three coils reverses the field and so the direction of rotation.

A cage rotor is simple, rugged and low-maintenance, with no brushes or slip rings; a wound rotor gives higher starting torque and speed control by external resistance, at more upkeep. Light load gives a poor power factor.
Cage induction motors suit constant-speed work such as fans, pumps, conveyors and compressors; their speed is hard to control without a drive and their starting current is high.
Induction motors are used on ships for pumps, fans and compressors up to 700 kW or more, totally enclosed; the UK chose an induction motor to drive its Type 45 destroyer.
A three-phase motor run from a single phase will not self-start but can be hand started; a motor already running when one phase is lost heats very quickly and must be taken off by its protection.
In one long-run record of motor failures, overloads were 30%, single-phasing 14% and bearing failure 13%; worn starter contacts are given as the most common cause of single-phasing.

An insulation resistance test shows a wet or contaminated motor or a dead short to earth but cannot prove it good; a winding resistance test compares phases, and under 1% difference is typical of a good winding.
His sheet says a brushless motor is safe for hazardous areas; a maker builds hazardous-area motors to prevent ignition and certifies them to ATEX and IECEx.
notes.contested: Dan's sheet treats the absence of brushes as making these motors safe in hazardous areas; a maker presents certified, purpose-built motors for these areas.

notes.claim: Slip is the fraction (synchronous speed minus actual speed) divided by synchronous speed: 0 at synchronous speed, 1 (100%) at standstill or locked rotor.

Read the pole count from the nameplate speed: on 50 Hz a two-pole field turns at 3000 rpm and a four-pole one at 1500, and the full-load speed on the nameplate is a little below that. A 1500 r/min, four-pole motor is a maker's standard 50 Hz line. Dan's sheet motor, 5.5 kW at 2950 rpm, is therefore two-pole at 50 Hz (computed: slip (3000 - 2950) / 3000 = 1.67%).
The ABB 0.75 kW four-pole data sheet gives a rated speed of 1437 r/min on 50 Hz, so its full-load slip is (1500 - 1437) / 1500 = 4.2% (computed).
Slip is proportional to the load: a motor at half load has slip halfway between its full-load slip and zero.
When load goes up the rotor slows, slip grows, and rotor current and torque grow with it until the motor's torque balances the load's. At small slip the torque is directly proportional to slip.
The rotor current's frequency is slip times the supply frequency, so at full load (slip 5% or less) it is only a few hertz: 2.5 Hz on a 50 Hz supply at 5% slip.

Light-load power factor is poor because the magnetising current stays almost the same while the useful current falls. ABB's 0.75 kW four-pole motor draws 1.4 A with no load against 1.90 A at full load, with power factor 0.7 at full load and 0.49 at half load. Below about half load the power factor degrades quickly.

The ABB 0.75 kW four-pole data sheet gives a starting current of 5.9 times rated, a locked-rotor torque of 3.5 times rated and a maximum (breakdown) torque of 3.8 times rated. The starting current is high because a locked rotor is like a shorted transformer secondary.
notes.contested: Starting torque of a direct-on-line cage motor: ABB's handbook gives 1.5 to 2.5 times rated for small motors, while the small ABB data sheet gives 3.5. It is a range that depends on the motor design, so read the data sheet for the motor in hand.

notes.claim: If the load torque goes beyond the motor's breakdown torque the motor slows further instead of settling: it stalls, the current stays at the locked-rotor level, and it overheats rapidly and risks insulation failure if not protected.

With one line open at standstill the rotating field collapses into a pulsing single-phase field, so a motor at rest hums and will not start. If the motor was already running and one line is lost, the two remaining line currents rise to about 173% of normal.

The minimum acceptable insulation resistance for a motor winding depends on the standard, the winding and its age: the older IEEE 43 rule is 1 megohm plus 1 megohm per kV; a widely quoted newer figure is 5 megohms for windings up to 1,000 V (WEG, citing IEEE 43); a maker or the standard in force sets the real value, and the trend counts as much as one reading.
notes.contested: The minimum insulation resistance for a motor: the older IEEE 43 rule (1 megohm plus 1 per kV), a newer 5 megohm figure for low-voltage windings, and a note that the real minimum depends on the insulation. The lesson should send him to the maker's figure rather than state one number.

notes.claim: Royal Navy ships have used a 440 V, 60 Hz, three-phase main supply since 1946 (four Daring class destroyers, in line with US Navy practice); it has been the preferred supply ever since. So a motor at sea usually runs on 60 Hz. (Added for i1, review fix: why the 60 Hz choice matters.)

A motor's overload relay is set to the motor's rated current, not its tripping current: it does not trip at 1.05 times the setting and trips at 1.2 times. An overloaded motor draws more than its rated current until the relay trips. (Added for i1, review fix: how an overload shows and what to check.)

The isolator closes the supply; Start (normally open, sprung) makes the coil circuit; the coil pulls in the main contacts, and a latching contact across Start keeps the coil fed once Start is released.
Stop (normally closed) breaks the coil circuit, and so does the overload's release contact after its bimetal strips bend; the coil drops out and the contacts release.

The coil does the pulling and holding of the main contacts; the latching contact's job is to keep the coil fed. (His sheet's item 7 words it as the latching contacts pulling and holding the main contacts.)

After a power cut the coil drops out and the motor stops; it does not restart by itself, because the holding contact has returned to open. A contactor with a holding contact gives low-voltage protection; maintained contacts give low-voltage release.
The overload's contacts sit in series with the coil and are operated by heat, not by the contactor's movement.
Overload relays protect against overload only: fuses or a breaker give the short-circuit protection, and a maker advises fuses with the thermal overload relay.
His coil is 230 V, fed from one phase and neutral; the coil rating must be right for how it is connected and for the supply voltage.
Direct-on-line starting is uncontrolled: full current and torque from the start. Start current is usually 6 to 8 times rated and can exceed 10 times.
His sheet gives DOL up to 5 kW; the web summary gives often under 4 kW; ABB says the limit depends on the area of use, and some utilities restrict DOL starting for motors of 5.5 kW or higher.
notes.contested: Rules of thumb for the largest DOL motor differ (5 kW, under 4 kW, 5.5 kW); the maker says it depends on the area of use and gives 5.5 kW as one utility limit.

notes.claim: DOL starters are used for compressors, pumps and fans; repeated stopping and starting can make the thermal overload operate.

Star-delta cuts starting current to about 30% (a third) and starting torque to about 25% of direct-on-line; the motor must be delta connected when running, and the starter uses three contactors, an overload and a timer.
Star-delta works only when the load is light at the start, and there are current peaks at the switch from star to delta.
His group's star-delta worked answer multiplies the star power by 3 to get the delta power.
The web summary's wording that DOL gives 100% of rated torque is loose: ABB gives full starting torque as 1.5 to 2.5 times rated for a small motor.
His group handout says that start buttons are wired in parallel.
Isolate and prove dead before work on a starter: the maker's own instruction is to disconnect power before any work on the equipment.

A contactor is rated for the motor it switches: for squirrel-cage motors (duty AC-3) it makes about 6 to 8 times the rated current when closing, or 5 to 7 on another maker's figure, and breaks only the rated current when opening; most contact wear comes from the making.
Restarting a motor before it has stopped turning can give a current peak up to twice that of a start from standstill, so a quick Stop-then-Start is hard on the contacts.
A DOL starter connects the motor straight to the supply at full voltage; the start current can cause voltage dips on the supply and heavy forces in the cables and the motor windings.

On a generator supply, DOL gives the highest inrush of any starting method, and the motor can develop several times full-load torque; on a ship the generator, not the starter, is the limit, and large motors starting one after another during manoeuvring can cause severe voltage dips.

Star-delta puts each winding on 1/sqrt(3) of the line voltage while starting; the changeover can briefly open the supply and give a current spike, which on one generator maker's figures can be as high as 5 x run kVA if it is badly timed, but ABB says is typically lower than a DOL start.
notes.contested: Sources differ on the size of the star-to-delta changeover spike: ABB says typically lower than a DOL start; a generator maker warns it can reach 5 x run kVA if the changeover is not set well.

notes.claim: The overload relay is set to the motor's rated current, not its trip current: no trip at 1.05 times the setting, trip at 1.2 times; it also protects against phase failure, and it has no power contacts so it can only work through the contactor.
After an overload trip the relay will not reset until it has cooled, which lets the motor cool before it is restarted.

The contactor coil must have the right voltage: the usual limits are 0.85 to 1.1 times its rating; too low a voltage can fail to close it, make it chatter and melt the coil, and too high a voltage can burn it out.

A buzzing or chattering contactor points to low or unstable coil voltage, a poor control connection, a wrong coil, dirty or unseated magnet faces, or a damaged shading ring; check the voltage across the coil terminals while it is closing.

A contactor can hold line voltage even when its coil circuit is off, so isolate and prove dead before touching a starter: prove all supply conductors dead, with a voltage indicator that is proved before and after use.
Several Stop buttons go in series (any one stops the motor) and several Start buttons in parallel with the holding contact (any one starts it).
A drive has three parts: a rectifier turns AC to DC, a DC bus with capacitors smooths it, and an inverter switches it back to AC at chosen frequency and voltage by pulse-width modulation.
Motor speed follows the supply frequency, so a drive that sets the frequency sets the speed.
Voltage is lowered in proportion to frequency so the flux stays constant (constant V/f); otherwise the motor draws excessive current at low frequency, with saturation.

Below the nominal frequency is the constant flux range; above it the voltage can rise no further and the motor is in field weakening, where it can run at constant power, so maximum torque falls with frequency.
A drive's soft start removes the inrush of a direct start and the mechanical shock.
For fans and pumps power varies roughly as the cube of speed: half speed needs about one eighth power in theory; a maker says treat the savings as theoretical.
Slowing a conveyor from 100% to 80% saves 20% of energy while a pump or fan saves nearer 50%, so savings are large only on variable-torque loads.
VFDs on ships are used on cranes, winches, bow thrusters, ventilation, pumps and compressors (a maker's list).
Fast-rising voltage pulses and high switching frequencies of modern drives can send current pulses through motor bearings that erode the races.
A drive trip on over-voltage during stopping can come from regenerated energy: the fix named is a longer deceleration time or a brake chopper; harmonics can also overcharge the DC link capacitors.
Earth-fault trips are found from the sum of the output currents and often from weak or damp insulation; disconnect the drive before an insulation resistance test on the motor and cable.
One single-phase winding makes a pulsating field, not a turning one, so it gives no starting torque; a three-phase motor on one phase will not self-start but can be hand started either way.

A start winding at 90 electrical degrees, with thinner wire and fewer turns, has higher resistance and lower inductance, so its current shifts less than the main winding's; the two currents are out of step and the field turns.
The angle between the two currents in a split-phase motor is about 30 degrees.
Starting torque goes with the currents and the sine of the angle between them.
A centrifugal switch drops the start winding out: at 3/4 of synchronous speed (Kuphaldt), about 75% of running speed (his sheet), approximately 80% of full speed (MSU).

Split-phase starting torque is low and suits easily started loads and fractional horsepower, up to 1/3 horsepower (250 W); typical figures are 100 to 175% of rated torque and 700 to 1,000% of rated current.
The start winding is not rated for continuous use, so frequent starts or a long start can overheat and burn it out.
Once started the auxiliary winding is optional; the main winding alone keeps the motor running.
The direction is set by reversing the leads of one winding (start or main) before starting.
A capacitor in series with the start winding makes that winding's current lead the supply voltage, while the main winding's current still lags, so the angle between the currents grows.
The angle is almost 80 degrees against about 30 degrees in a split-phase motor; ideally the capacitor is chosen so the start winding's current leads the main winding's by 90 degrees at startup.
Starting torque goes with the sine of the angle between the currents, so going from 30 to 80 degrees alone raises starting torque to nearly twice that of a split-phase motor.
A capacitor-start motor has moderate starting torque, higher than split-phase, and the phase shift is greater.
The centrifugal switch takes the start winding and capacitor out at about 75 to 80% of speed.
The motor then runs on the main winding alone. His sheet credits 'momentum from the startup'; the fuller source says the auxiliary winding is optional once started.
A permanent-split capacitor motor keeps a continuously energised auxiliary winding and has no centrifugal switch; a larger capacitor can be used just for starting if switched out at speed.
A failed capacitor is one of the most common causes of a motor that hums but will not start; compare a measured capacitor value with its marked rating.
In a series motor the same current flows through field and armature.

A turning armature makes a back emf opposing the supply; it is zero at standstill, so a motor not yet turning draws maximum current, and a load that slows it drops the back emf and raises the current.
The armature current is limited at start by armature resistance alone, so an external starting resistance is placed in series with the armature.
The motor's back emf is the supply voltage less the voltage lost in the resistance.
In its linear (unsaturated) region a series motor's torque goes with the square of the armature current, so it has very high starting torque.
Remove the load and the current falls, the field weakens, and the speed rises towards destruction: series motors must have overspeed protection and be coupled directly, never belt driven.
A shunt or compound motor can be run safely with no load but a series motor cannot.
A series motor suits crane hoists, elevators and large excavators, where a high starting torque is crucial.
A universal motor can operate on either AC or DC power and uses an electromagnet as its stator.
In a shunt motor the field is across the supply, so its current and flux stay steady.
A heavier load slows the motor, which lowers the back emf, lets more armature current flow and raises the torque; the speed settles a little lower than before.
His sheet says the extra current makes the motor 'speed back up to compensate'; the fuller sources say the speed falls off as the load increases.
notes.contested: Dan's sheet says a loaded shunt motor speeds back up to compensate; textbooks say its speed is nearly constant but falls off as load increases.

notes.claim: Speed regulation is the change in speed from no load to full load divided by the full-load speed; sources differ: his sheet 10 to 20%, IDC 7 to 10%, one site puts the armature drop at about 5%.
notes.contested: Sources differ on how far a shunt motor's speed falls between no load and full load: 10-20% (his sheet), 7-10% (IDC), about 5% (a circuits site).

notes.claim: Weakening the field raises the speed: a rheostat in series with the shunt field gives speeds above rated, and is the usual method.
Start a shunt motor with the field rheostat in the slow-speed position, so the field current is at its maximum: starting torque goes with field current.
Lower starting torque than a series motor: his sheet and a text say so, while Rose-Hulman says the starting torque is as high as in the series motor.
notes.contested: Whether a shunt motor's starting torque is lower than a series motor's: his sheet and PEG-3722 say lower; Rose-Hulman says as high.

notes.claim: A shunt motor has a safe no-load speed as long as the field is not de-energised; if the field fails the speed can run away, so loss-of-field protection is usual.
Brushes and commutator need regular maintenance.
Shunt motors suit constant-speed work such as machine tools and pumps.
A compound motor has both a series and a shunt field winding.
In a cumulative compound motor the series and shunt fields work together, with fluxes in the same direction; in a differential one they oppose.
A shunt coil added to a series motor limits the top speed at light load, and a cumulative compound motor has a definite no-load speed and can run safely with no load.
A cumulative compound motor has more starting torque than a shunt motor and steadier speed than a series motor, but not as steady as a shunt motor.
A differential compound motor is rarely used because it can run unstably when the load changes; because the series flux opposes the shunt flux, flux falls with load and the speed can rise with load.
A long-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the supply with the series winding between it and the armature; a short-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the armature only.
Compound motors suit presses, shears, crushers and reciprocating compressors.
